rules.name: Block abuse of exploited vulnerable signed drivers
rules.hint: Stops apps from saving known-vulnerable signed drivers that attackers use to reach the kernel. Standard protection rule.
rules.description: Prevents applications from writing vulnerable signed drivers (drivers with known flaws that malware and some cheats load to get kernel access) to disk. Drivers that are already installed are not affected; the Microsoft vulnerable driver blocklist covers loading. Microsoft lists it as a standard protection rule that can go straight to Block.
rules.gamerImpact: None for games or anti-cheat. Old RGB, fan-control or overclocking tools that ship a known-vulnerable driver may fail to install it.

rules.name: Block credential stealing from the Windows local security authority subsystem
rules.hint: Stops processes from reading LSASS memory to steal passwords. Redundant with LSA protection; frequent harmless blocks are normal.
rules.description: Blocks processes from opening the Local Security Authority (LSASS) process with memory-read access, the technique credential dumpers use. When LSA protection is on, the rule adds no extra protection but does no harm. Expect block events for svchost.exe, updaters and monitoring tools: they are only denied access to LSASS memory, not stopped from running. Warn mode is not supported.
rules.gamerImpact: None. Block events for Windows services and launcher updaters are expected noise that Microsoft says can be ignored; nothing stops working.
rules.notes: Redundant when LSA protection (sec.lsa-protection) is on. Limited exclusion support.

rules.name: Block persistence through WMI event subscription
rules.hint: Stops malware from hiding a restart trigger in WMI event subscriptions. Standard protection rule with no effect on games.
rules.description: Blocks the creation of permanent WMI event subscriptions, a fileless persistence technique where malware keeps its trigger in the WMI repository instead of on disk. Microsoft lists it as a standard protection rule; the only known conflict is the Configuration Manager client, which home PCs do not use.
rules.gamerImpact: None for games. Only tools that create permanent WMI event subscriptions are affected, which consumer software rarely does.
rules.notes: Test in Audit first on PCs managed by Configuration Manager. Limited exclusion support.

rules.name: Block executable content from email client and webmail
rules.hint: Blocks programs, scripts and archives that come straight from Outlook or webmail. Part of the gaming-safe baseline.
rules.description: Stops executable files (exe, dll, scr), scripts (ps1, vbs, js) and archives opened from Outlook, Outlook.com and other popular webmail services from running. Malicious attachments are still one of the most common ways malware arrives. iG Windows Tuner's gaming-safe baseline (sec.asr-baseline) already sets it to Block.
rules.gamerImpact: None for games. Executable attachments opened from mail are blocked; save them through a browser download if you trust the sender.

rules.name: Block JavaScript or VBScript from launching downloaded executable content
rules.hint: Stops JavaScript and VBScript droppers from starting programs they downloaded. Part of the gaming-safe baseline.
rules.description: Malware written in JavaScript or VBScript often only downloads and starts the real payload. This rule blocks scripts from launching executables they fetched from the internet. A few old installers use such a script stub, but games and launchers do not. iG Windows Tuner's gaming-safe baseline already sets it to Block.
rules.gamerImpact: None for games. Old installers that use a VBScript or JScript stub to download and start an exe may fail.

rules.name: Block execution of potentially obfuscated scripts
rules.hint: Blocks scripts (including PowerShell) that look deliberately obfuscated. Needs cloud protection. Part of the gaming-safe baseline.
rules.description: Detects suspicious properties of obfuscated scripts, which malware uses to hide what it does. It covers PowerShell and relies on AMSI and cloud-delivered protection, so it only works fully with cloud protection on. iG Windows Tuner's gaming-safe baseline already sets it to Block.
rules.gamerImpact: Low. A few mod installers or tweak scripts that pack their code can be blocked; games and launchers themselves are not affected.

rules.name: Block untrusted and unsigned processes that run from USB
rules.hint: Blocks unsigned or untrusted programs started directly from USB sticks and SD cards. Part of the gaming-safe baseline.
rules.description: Prevents unsigned or untrusted executable files from running from removable drives, including SD cards. Copying files from the drive still works; files copied to the disk are judged where they run. iG Windows Tuner's gaming-safe baseline already sets it to Block.
rules.gamerImpact: Low. Unsigned portable tools started straight from a USB stick are blocked; signed programs and copying files are not affected.

rules.name: Block rebooting machine in Safe Mode
rules.hint: Stops tools such as bcdedit from forcing the next boot into Safe Mode, a ransomware trick. Safe Mode stays available from Recovery.
rules.description: Ransomware sometimes restarts Windows in Safe Mode, where many security products do not run, before encrypting files. This rule blocks commonly abused commands such as bcdedit and bootcfg from setting a Safe Mode boot. You can still reach Safe Mode through the Windows Recovery Environment (Settings > System > Recovery > Advanced startup).
rules.gamerImpact: None for games. Troubleshooting guides that set Safe Mode with bcdedit will not work; use Advanced startup instead.
rules.notes: Microsoft lists it under the rules to test in Audit first.

rules.name: Block use of copied or impersonated system tools
rules.hint: Blocks copies of Windows system tools run from other folders. Heuristics can flag apps in custom install folders: audit first.
rules.description: Treats the programs in System32 and SysWOW64 as Windows system tools and blocks copies or same-named files that run from other locations, even when signed. Microsoft notes that its heuristics can also flag legitimate third-party programs that run from non-default install paths. Audit first and add a per-rule exclusion for any trusted program it reports.
rules.gamerImpact: Medium. Games, launchers or tools installed in custom folders can match the heuristics; check the audit view before switching to Block.

rules.name: Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion
rules.hint: Blocks new or rare programs until Microsoft's cloud trusts them. Strong, but hits fresh game patches and mods. Audit or Warn first.
rules.description: Blocks executable files that are not yet prevalent, old enough or on a trusted list, judged by cloud-delivered protection. Brand-new malware is caught this way, but so is any legitimate program that few people have run yet. Cloud protection must be on. Use Audit or Warn and review the audit view before considering Block.
rules.gamerImpact: High. Freshly patched games, indie and beta builds, mod managers and community tools can be blocked until their reputation builds up.

rules.name: Use advanced protection against ransomware
rules.hint: Extra ransomware heuristics that also block unsigned, little-known files until they earn reputation. Needs cloud protection.
rules.description: Uses client and cloud heuristics to decide whether a file resembles ransomware. Signed files, files the cloud knows to be clean and prevalent files are not blocked, but unknown files without a positive reputation can be. Such blocks usually clear as reputation grows. Cloud protection must be on.
rules.gamerImpact: Medium. Unsigned, little-known executables such as new indie games, mods or trainers can be blocked until they gain reputation. Audit first.

rules.name: Block process creations originating from PSExec and WMI commands
rules.hint: Blocks programs started through PsExec or WMI, which malware uses to spread. Some launchers and admin tools use WMI too: audit first.
rules.description: PsExec and WMI can start programs remotely, and malware uses them for command and control or to spread across a network. This rule blocks every process created that way. Some legitimate software, including updaters, hardware utilities and management scripts, also starts processes through WMI, so test it in Audit first.
rules.gamerImpact: Medium. Launchers, updaters or hardware utilities that start helpers through WMI can break. Check the audit view before using Block.
rules.notes: Never enable on PCs managed by Configuration Manager. Limited exclusion support.

rules.name: Block all Office applications from creating child processes
rules.hint: Stops Word, Excel, PowerPoint, OneNote and Access from starting other programs, the classic macro-malware path. Office only.
rules.description: Malicious documents usually run macros or exploit code that starts PowerShell, cmd or a downloaded payload. This rule blocks Office apps from creating child processes. Some add-ins and business macros do this legitimately, so audit first. It is only enforced when Office is installed under Program Files.
rules.gamerImpact: None for games. Office add-ins or macros that start Command Prompt, PowerShell or helper apps are blocked.

rules.name: Block Office applications from creating executable content
rules.hint: Stops Office apps and their macros from writing programs to disk and running them, a persistence trick. Office only.
rules.description: Prevents Word, Excel and PowerPoint from saving malicious components to disk where they survive a restart, and blocks running untrusted files that macros wrote. It does not depend on where Office is installed. Audit first if you rely on macros that generate files.
rules.gamerImpact: None for games. Only Office documents and macros that save and run executable files are affected.

rules.name: Block Office applications from injecting code into other processes
rules.hint: Blocks Office apps from injecting code into other processes. No legitimate use is known. No Warn mode; restart Office after a change.
rules.description: Attackers inject code from Office into other processes so it runs disguised as a clean program. Microsoft knows of no legitimate business purpose for this. The rule applies to Word, Excel, OneNote and PowerPoint installed under Program Files, needs an Office restart to take effect and does not support Warn mode.
rules.gamerImpact: None for games. A few security products (BeyondTrust Privilege Guard, Heimdal) are listed by Microsoft as incompatible.

rules.name: Block Office communication application from creating child processes
rules.hint: Stops Outlook from starting other programs while keeping normal Outlook features. Protects against rules and forms exploits.
rules.description: Prevents Outlook from creating child processes, which blocks social-engineering payloads and the Outlook rules and forms exploits attackers use with stolen credentials. Normal mail features keep working. It is only enforced when Office is installed under Program Files.
rules.gamerImpact: None for games. Outlook add-ins that start external programs are blocked.

rules.name: Block Win32 API calls from Office macros
rules.hint: Stops VBA macros from calling Windows APIs directly, which fileless macro malware uses. Most macros never need it. Office only.
rules.description: Office VBA can call Win32 APIs, which malware abuses to launch shellcode without writing files. The rule blocks those calls from macros. Most people who use macros at all never need Win32 API calls, but audit first if you run complex business macros.
rules.gamerImpact: None for games. Only Office macros that call Windows APIs are affected.

rules.name: Block Adobe Reader from creating child processes
rules.hint: Stops Adobe Reader from starting other programs, a common exploit path in malicious PDFs. Only matters if Reader is installed.
rules.description: Malicious PDFs use social engineering or exploits to make Adobe Reader download and start a payload. Blocking Reader from creating child processes stops that path. Reader plug-ins or workflows that open other programs can be affected, so audit first if you depend on them.
rules.gamerImpact: None for games. Only Adobe Reader workflows that start other programs are affected.

rules.name: Block Webshell creation for Servers
rules.hint: Exchange servers only. Not applicable to Windows 11; leave it Not configured, as Microsoft advises.
rules.description: Blocks web shell scripts on Windows servers that run Microsoft Exchange. It does not apply to Windows 11 clients, and Microsoft advises leaving it Not configured outside Defender for Endpoint management to avoid conflicts. iG Windows Tuner shows it for completeness and does not change it.
rules.gamerImpact: None. The rule only applies to Exchange servers.
